description: Questions whose answers we already know, run before any real transcript is judged. Each state is hand-written so its reading is unambiguous to a human; if the classifier cannot separate these, nothing it says about a real review is worth printing. Pairs are deliberate — the same check against a state that should pass and one that should fail — because a classifier that answers 'pass' to everything would otherwise calibrate perfectly.

items.name: asks about frequency
items.state:
The per-star spring is lively, and whether that is right depends on something this file does not tell me: how often do readers actually rate books? If this is a once-per-title action it is fine as it stands. If people are rating dozens of titles in a shelving session, this wants to be much quieter. Can you tell me which it is?

FINDINGS
NONE

items.name: reports the composite against the screen
items.state:
Each of these five composables is individually fine. The problem is the screen: applying a discount moves the total, slides in a badge, shifts the postage note, brightens the loyalty line and recolours the button, all at once, so nothing tells the eye what just happened. Decide what the event is about and let that lead.

items.name: leaves the framework path alone
items.state:
The NavHost needs nothing: Navigation already installs a predictive-back handler and seeks the transition with SeekableTransitionState, so back gestures follow the finger without any app code.
